title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the ear to the words

questions.prompt: Five people are asked "Do you like rap?". Put their answers in order, from the coldest to the most enthusiastic.

options.text: I quite like it.
I'm crazy about it.
I can't stand it.
I like it very much.
I don't really like it.

questions.explanation: English grades a taste as finely as a thermometer. "I can't stand it" is the coldest of the five: it says the speaker hates rap. "I don't really like it" softens the same refusal into something polite. "I quite like it" crosses over to approval, but mild approval — do not hear enthusiasm in it just because the word "quite" looks strong. "I like it very much" is plain, strong liking. And "I'm crazy about it", like "I'm mad about it", sits at the top of the ladder. Choosing the right rung is what makes an opinion sound sincere.

questions.prompt: Paraphrase this sentence in your own words: "Within three years she had won worldwide renown." Which sentence does the job?

options.text: She spent three years looking for fame abroad.
Three years later she was still unknown outside her own country.
She won three international prizes in as many years.
In three years she became famous all over the world.

questions.explanation: A paraphrase keeps the whole meaning and borrows no word: renown becomes famous, worldwide becomes all over the world, within three years becomes in three years. The three others change the meaning instead of changing the words — one turns a success into a search, one turns it into a failure, and one invents prizes the sentence never mentions. Say it again, say it all, say it differently: that is the test.

questions.prompt: In which pair do the two words contain the SAME vowel sound?

options.text: coat – snow
break – bread
wait – wild
love – prove

questions.explanation: Coat and snow both carry the [ou] of home, spelt "oa" in one and "ow" in the other — one sound written two ways, which is the whole difficulty of English vowels. Break has the [ei] of name while bread has the short vowel of red, although the two share the letters "ea"; wait has [ei] and wild the vowel of my; and love and prove look like a rhyming pair on the page and share nothing at all in the ear. Never trust the letters one by one: group them, then listen.

questions.prompt: Your teacher is going to play a song once, and asks you to circle, in a printed list of twelve words, the ones you hear. What do you do first?

options.text: Write down every word you understand as it goes past.
Look the twelve words up in a dictionary.
Listen for the story and leave the list for the second playing.
Read the twelve words before the music starts.

questions.explanation: You cannot recognise a word you have never read, and a song does not wait: the twelve words must be in your head before the first note. Writing down everything you understand is impossible at singing speed, and every word you write costs you the line that follows. A dictionary costs the very minutes you need. And keeping the list for a second playing throws away the one playing you have been given. Read the task first, then listen — in that order, always.

questions.prompt: The rules of a music festival say: "Under-16s can come in free, but they mustn't stay after ten o'clock." Which statement follows from the rules?

options.text: Under-16s have to pay, and they may then stay as long as they like.
A girl of fifteen gets in free and has to leave by ten.
A girl of fifteen pays nothing and may stay until midnight.
Under-16s are not allowed into the festival at all.
Under-16s pay half price and may stay until the end.

questions.explanation: The two modals share the work between them: can grants a permission — free entry for anyone under sixteen — and mustn't takes one away, so ten o'clock is a limit and not a suggestion. A girl of fifteen therefore pays nothing and leaves by ten. Reading mustn't as "need not" produces the girl who stays until midnight; ignoring can produces the ones who pay, pay half or are turned away at the door. Two modals, two different jobs, and both of them have to be read.

questions.prompt: A critic writes that a young singer "has the prowess but not yet the renown". What is he saying?

options.text: She is already famous, but she does not sing well.
She neither sings well nor is known to anybody.
She sings very well but is not famous yet.
She sings well and is famous, but only at home.

questions.explanation: Prowess is great skill and renown is fame, so the critic is separating two things the public usually confuses: the voice is already there, the name is not. The other readings swap the two words round, deny both of them, or add a limit — only at home — that the sentence does not carry. "But not yet" is worth a second look as well: it announces that the fame is expected to follow.
